findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define the exact match vocabulary (regex or closed term list) for 'test reference' and 'verification phrase' in R1, so the blocking trigger is deterministic and reproducible across implementations.
evidence: Plan text: 'a leaf plan must have >= 1 `- [ ]` AC item containing a backtick command, test reference, or verification phrase'
Neither 'test reference' nor 'verification phrase' is further defined — no regex, no lexicon, no examples given.
The existing codebase (det_lint._verify_command_strings) scans for backtick content AND 'Verify:'/'Proof:' prefixes globally, but R1 is scoped to AC item lines and must define its own vocabulary.
R1 is a BLOCKING check; ambiguity in what triggers a pass causes either systematic FPs (real plans blocked) or FNs (the check never fires on genuinely bare ACs).
findings.finding: The R1 blocking check's trigger vocabulary — 'test reference' and 'verification phrase' — is undefined, leaving a critical design choice to the implementer for a check that will block plans.
findings.location: Approach section, R1 description: 'a backtick command, test reference, or verification phrase'
scenarios: An AC item like '- [ ] Run `src/rebar/foo.py` to regenerate the schema.' contains a backtick but it is a file path, not a command — does it pass R1?
An AC item like '- [ ] Verified by observing no exception in the log.' contains a 'verification phrase' in natural language — is that in scope?
Two implementers reading this plan independently will produce different regex patterns, one of which may have unacceptable FP/FN rates.
findings.suggested_fix: Specify R1's AC-item scan as: (a) any inline code span (backtick-wrapped token) that matches a command shape (e.g. contains `/`, `pytest`, `rebar`, or `make`); (b) a closed list of verification-phrase prefixes such as 'checked:', 'verified:', 'confirmed:'; or alternatively state that R1 reuses the existing `_verify_command_strings` logic filtered to AC-item lines (since that function already extracts backtick content from AC lines).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Clarify whether the 30-char proximity for `etc.` is measured on the ORIGINAL AC line (before code-span stripping) or on the stripped version, and specify the two-pass order: (1) find `etc.` positions on the original, (2) check proximity to code-span positions on the original, (3) then strip spans for the remaining vague-term matches.
evidence: Plan text: 'strip inline code spans before matching, scope to AC item lines via det_operator_attested.ac_item_lines … keep `etc.` with a code-span-proximity exemption (within 30 chars)'
Stripping code spans (e.g. via `_INLINE_CODE_RE.sub(...)`) removes the spans from the string before matching — there is nothing to measure distance from on the stripped text.

The existing `_plan_clarity.py` uses `_INLINE_CODE_RE.sub(' CODE ', line)` to preserve a placeholder; if R2 uses the same placeholder, proximity becomes 'within 30 chars of the literal string CODE' — which changes meaning depending on original code-span length.
The two-step order — 'strip then match' vs 'measure proximity then strip' — determines correctness and neither is specified.
findings.finding: The `etc.` code-span proximity exemption measures distance ambiguously: after stripping inline code spans the code span no longer exists in the text, making 'within 30 chars of a code span' unmeasurable on the stripped string.
findings.location: Approach section, R2: 'keep `etc.` with a code-span-proximity exemption (within 30 chars)'
scenarios: AC item: '- [ ] Run the pipeline, etc. (see `rebar run --dry-run`)' — the code span is 22 chars after `etc.`. On the original string, proximity passes. After stripping, `etc.` is 10 chars from 'CODE'; the answer depends on which string is used.

AC item: '- [ ] Etc. and other `long-command-with-many-args`' — etc. is 10 chars before the span on the original but 10 chars before 'CODE' on the stripped version, accidentally both passing — but only by coincidence.
findings.suggested_fix: Measure `etc.` proximity on the ORIGINAL line before stripping: record all `[start, end]` code-span positions via a first-pass regex scan, then check whether any `etc.` occurrence falls within 30 chars of a span boundary; only then strip and match the remaining vague terms.
